books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

stimulus.source_note: Homestead Act, May 20, 1862, Section 1. Public domain.
stimulus.text: That any person who is the head of a family, or who has arrived at the age of twenty-one years, and is a citizen of the United States... shall... be entitled to enter one quarter section or a less quantity of unappropriated public lands...

source: original; stimulus is a verbatim excerpt from the Homestead Act, May 20, 1862, Section 1, public domain
stem: The Homestead Act's requirement that a claimant be a head of family or at least twenty-one most directly shows that the law was meant to

options.text: give land only to soldiers who had served in the Civil War.
options.misconception: The act barred those who had borne arms against the United States; it did not limit land to Union soldiers.

options.text: keep all western land in the hands of the federal government.
options.misconception: The act gave public land away to settlers; it did not keep it federal.

options.text: reserve western land for large railroad companies.
options.misconception: Railroads got land under separate grants; the Homestead Act gave small plots to individual settlers.

options.text: settle the West with independent farming households.

rationales.A: The act excluded those who had fought against the United States; it was not limited to soldiers, and most claimants were civilians.
rationales.B: The act transferred public land into private hands; it did the opposite of keeping land federal.
rationales.C: Railroad land came from separate grants, such as the Pacific Railway Act; the Homestead Act gave a quarter section — 160 acres — to a settler. Background: the act required five years of residence and cultivation before a patent issued.
rationales.D: Heads of families and adults over twenty-one, claiming 160 acres to live on and farm, are the building blocks of farming households.
rationales.general:
1. Read who could claim land. A head of family, or any adult over twenty-one who was a citizen or intended to become one.
2. Read how much land. One quarter section — 160 acres — a family farm, not a plantation or a railroad grant.
3. Put the two together. The law pictures the West filled with households farming their own plots.
Remember: a law's fine print is its picture of the future. Here the future is small farms run by families, not companies or armies.
